title: Conduction
lead: A tile floor feels colder than a carpet at the same temperature because it draws heat out of your foot faster, and this section explains why. Heat is conducted by molecular collisions at a rate that grows with the temperature difference and the area of contact and falls with the thickness of the material, and a constant of the material, its thermal conductivity, sets the scale; the equation that holds these four factors together tells how much ice a Styrofoam box lets melt in a day and how small a temperature difference an aluminum pan needs to boil water.
objectives: Observe conduction of heat in collisions.
Study thermal conductivities of common substances.
summary_html:
• Heat conduction is the transfer of heat between two objects in direct contact with each other.
  • The rate of heat transfer $\kQh/\kt$ (energy per unit time) is proportional to the temperature difference $\kTemptwo - \kTempone$ and the contact area $A$ and inversely proportional to the distance $d$ between the objects: $$\frac{\kQh}{\kt} = \frac{kA(\kTemptwo - \kTempone)}{d}.$$
notes: Figure 14.15, the insulated wall at the head of the section, is left out; Figure 14.20, the walrus, is left out with its problem, which the book does not key; the seven problems the book leaves unkeyed are left out; and the book’s own slip in Example 14.6, where the water that evaporates is said to melt, is kept as printed.

figures.original_caption: The molecules in two bodies at different temperatures have different average kinetic energies. Collisions occurring at the contact surface tend to transfer energy from high-temperature regions to low-temperature regions. In this illustration, a molecule in the lower temperature region (right side) has low energy before collision, but its energy increases after colliding with the contact surface. In contrast, a molecule in the higher temperature region (left side) has high energy before collision, but its energy decreases after colliding with the contact surface.

Heat conduction occurs through any material, represented here by a rectangular bar, whether window glass or walrus blubber. The temperature of the material is T2 on the left and T1 on the right, where T2 is greater than T1. The rate of heat transfer by conduction is directly proportional to the surface area A, the temperature difference T2 − T1, and the substance’s conductivity k. The rate of heat transfer is inversely proportional to the thickness d.

exercises.prompt: How does the rate of heat transfer by conduction change when all spatial dimensions are doubled?

answer.solution: Because area is the product of two spatial dimensions, it increases by a factor of four when each dimension is doubled $(A_{\text{final}} = (2d)^2 = 4d^2 = 4A_{\text{initial}})$. The distance, however, simply doubles. Because the temperature difference and the coefficient of thermal conductivity are independent of the spatial dimensions, the rate of heat transfer by conduction increases by a factor of four divided by two, or two: $$\left(\frac{\kQh}{\kt}\right)_{\text{final}} = \frac{kA_{\text{final}}(\kTemptwo - \kTempone)}{d_{\text{final}}} = \frac{k(4A_{\text{initial}})(\kTemptwo - \kTempone)}{2d_{\text{initial}}} = 2\frac{kA_{\text{initial}}(\kTemptwo - \kTempone)}{d_{\text{initial}}} = 2\left(\frac{\kQh}{\kt}\right)_{\text{initial}}.$$

exercises.prompt: Some electric stoves have a flat ceramic surface with heating elements hidden beneath. A pot placed over a heating element will be heated, while it is safe to touch the surface only a few centimeters away. Why is ceramic, with a conductivity less than that of a metal but greater than that of a good insulator, an ideal choice for the stove top?

answer.solution: The stove top has two jobs that pull in opposite directions. Straight up through the ceramic, from the element to the pot, heat must pass quickly, and a thin plate with a conductivity of about $0.84\ \text{J/s}\cdot\text{m}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C}$ conducts a large rate through a small thickness once the temperature difference across it builds up. Sideways along the plate, heat must not spread, and here the same conductivity has to carry heat over a distance of centimeters rather than millimeters, so the rate falls with the much greater distance and the surface a few centimeters away stays cool enough to touch. A metal would carry the heat sideways as readily as upward and the whole surface would become hot, while a good insulator would pass so little heat upward that the pot would barely warm.

exercises.prompt: Loose-fitting white clothing covering most of the body is ideal for desert dwellers, both in the hot Sun and during cold evenings. Explain how such clothing is advantageous during both day and night.

answer.solution: Loose clothing traps a layer of still air between the cloth and the skin, and air is one of the poorest conductors in Table 14.3, so the layer slows conduction in whichever direction the temperature difference points. In the hot Sun the air outside and the sunlit cloth are hotter than the body, and the trapped air limits the rate at which that heat is conducted inward; the white color also reflects most of the sunlight rather than absorbing it. In the cold evening the body is the hotter side, and the same layer of air limits the rate at which the body’s heat is conducted outward, just as thick clothing does in winter. Because the cloth covers most of the body, the layer of air is large and the skin is shaded and sheltered all day.

exercises.prompt: For the experiment that you devised in Example 14.1, which variables can be changed, and how should they be changed, so as to shorten the time in which a measurement is made?

options: Use a smaller quantity of ice (smaller $m$).
Use containers with smaller surface areas (smaller $A$).
Use a lower ambient temperature outside the container (smaller $\kTemptwo$).
answer.hint: The time to melt the ice is the heat it needs, $mL_{\text{f}}$, divided by the rate at which heat is conducted in. Ask which change makes that time shorter.

exercises.prompt: With reference to the experiment that you devised in Example 14.1, why does the change in the temperature of the ice indicate that it has entirely melted?

answer.solution: While ice and water are present together, the heat conducted into the container goes into the phase change, $\kQh = mL_{\text{f}}$, and the mixture stays at $0^\circ\text{C}$; the temperature cannot rise until the last of the ice has melted. Once the temperature of the contents begins to climb, the heat is going into warming the water, $\kQh = mc\kdTemp$, which means there is no ice left to absorb it. The first rise of the thermometer therefore marks the moment the ice has entirely melted, and the time up to that moment is the time the measurement needs.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the rate of conductive heat transfer for a substance?

options: The rate decreases with increased surface area and decreased thickness.
The rate increases with increased temperature difference and surface area.
The rate increases with decreased temperature difference and increased thickness.
The rate decreases with decreased temperature difference and increased surface area.
answer.hint: In $\kQh/\kt = kA(\kTemptwo - \kTempone)/d$, the area and the temperature difference are in the numerator and the thickness is in the denominator.

exercises.prompt: You wish to design a saucepan that has the same rate of thermal conduction as a pan made of silver. You need to use a less costly material, and limit the size of the pan so that the surface area in contact with a range heating element is no more than 50% greater than that of the hypothetical silver pan. Explain what other factor(s) can be adjusted, and by how much, so that your design will be successful. Use Table 14.3 to obtain thermal conductivity values for different substances.

answer.solution: The rate is $\kQh/\kt = kA(\kTemptwo - \kTempone)/d$, so with the same temperature difference the product $kA/d$ must be the same as for the silver pan. Silver has $k = 420\ \text{J/s}\cdot\text{m}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C}$; copper, at 390, is only 7% lower, and aluminum, at 220, is about half. Since the area may be at most 1.5 times that of the silver pan, the remaining factor is the thickness of the bottom. For copper, $kA/d$ matches with the same thickness if the area is made $420/390 = 1.08$ times as large, or with the same area if the bottom is made $390/420 = 0.93$ times as thick. For aluminum, the area alone is not enough, since $1.5 \times 220/420 = 0.79$, so the bottom must also be thinner, by the factor 0.79, or thinner still, $220/420 = 0.52$, if the area is kept the same. Any combination of a larger area up to the 50% limit and a thinner bottom that brings $kA/d$ back to the silver value will do.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the rate of heat conduction through house walls that are 13.0 cm thick and that have an average thermal conductivity twice that of glass wool. Assume there are no windows or doors. The surface area of the walls is $120\ \text{m}^2$ and their inside surface is at $18.0^\circ\text{C}$, while their outside surface is at $5.00^\circ\text{C}$. (b) How many 1-kW room heaters would be needed to balance the heat transfer due to conduction?

parts.hint: Take $k$ as twice the 0.042 of glass wool in Table 14.3 and put the thickness in meters.
Divide the rate by 1 kW and round up to a whole heater.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the rate of heat conduction out of the human body, assuming that the core internal temperature is $37.0^\circ\text{C}$, the skin temperature is $34.0^\circ\text{C}$, the thickness of the tissues between averages $1.00\ \text{cm}$, and the surface area is $1.40\ \text{m}^2$.

answer.hint: Use the conductivity of fatty tissue without blood from Table 14.3 and a temperature difference of $3.00^\circ\text{C}$.

exercises.prompt: A man consumes 3000 kcal of food in one day, converting most of it to maintain body temperature. If he loses half this energy by evaporating water (through breathing and sweating), how many kilograms of water evaporate?

answer.hint: Half of 3000 kcal, in joules, is the heat $\kQh = mL_{\text{v}}$; use the heat of vaporization at body temperature, 2430 kJ/kg, from Table 14.2.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the rate of heat conduction through the 3.00-cm-thick fur of a large animal having a $1.40\text{-m}^2$ surface area? Assume that the animal’s skin temperature is $32.0^\circ\text{C}$, that the air temperature is $-5.00^\circ\text{C}$, and that fur has the same thermal conductivity as air. (b) What food intake will the animal need in one day to replace this heat transfer?

parts.hint: The temperature difference across the fur is $37.0^\circ\text{C}$ and $k$ is that of air.
Multiply the rate by the seconds in a day to get joules, then divide by 4186 J/kcal.

exercises.prompt: Compare the rate of heat conduction through a 13.0-cm-thick wall that has an area of $10.0\ \text{m}^2$ and a thermal conductivity twice that of glass wool with the rate of heat conduction through a window that is 0.750 cm thick and that has an area of $2.00\ \text{m}^2$, assuming the same temperature difference across each.

answer.hint: With the same temperature difference the ratio of the rates is the ratio of $kA/d$ for the two, so no temperatures are needed.

exercises.prompt: Some stove tops are smooth ceramic for easy cleaning. If the ceramic is 0.600 cm thick and heat conduction occurs through the same area and at the same rate as computed in Example 14.6, what is the temperature difference across it? Ceramic has the same thermal conductivity as glass and brick.

answer.hint: Solve the conduction equation for $\kTemptwo - \kTempone$ with 2256 W, the pan’s area of $1.54 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^2$ and $k = 0.84$.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the rate of heat conduction through a double-paned window that has a $1.50\text{-m}^2$ area and is made of two panes of 0.800-cm-thick glass separated by a 1.00-cm air gap. The inside surface temperature is $15.0^\circ\text{C}$, while that on the outside is $-10.0^\circ\text{C}$. (Hint: There are identical temperature drops across the two glass panes. First find these and then the temperature drop across the air gap. This problem ignores the increased heat transfer in the air gap due to convection.) (b) Calculate the rate of heat conduction through a 1.60-cm-thick window of the same area and with the same temperatures. Compare your answer with that for part (a).

parts.hint: The same rate passes through each layer, so the temperature drops are in proportion to $d/k$ for each layer and add up to $25.0^\circ\text{C}$.
A single pane has no air gap; compare $kA\,\kdTemp/d$ for glass 1.60 cm thick with the answer to (a).

answer.solution: (a) 83 W (b) 24 times that of a double pane window.

exercises.prompt: For the human body, what is the rate of heat transfer by conduction through the body’s tissue with the following conditions: the tissue thickness is 3.00 cm, the change in temperature is $2.00^\circ\text{C}$, and the skin area is $1.50\ \text{m}^2$. How does this compare with the average heat transfer rate to the body resulting from an energy intake of about 2400 kcal per day? (No exercise is included.)

parts.hint: Use the conductivity of fatty tissue without blood and put the thickness in meters.
Turn 2400 kcal per day into watts by converting to joules and dividing by the seconds in a day, then take the ratio.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the rate of heat transfer by conduction through a window with an area of $1.00\ \text{m}^2$ that is 0.750 cm thick, if its inner surface is at $22.0^\circ\text{C}$ and its outer surface is at $35.0^\circ\text{C}$. (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which premise or assumption is responsible?

answer.hint: Use the conductivity of glass from Table 14.3 and a temperature difference of $13.0^\circ\text{C}$ across 0.00750 m.
answer.solution: (a) 1.46 kW (b) Very high power loss through a window. An electric heater of this power can keep an entire room warm. (c) The surface temperatures of the window do not differ by as great an amount as assumed. The inner surface will be warmer, and the outer surface will be cooler.
